summary: The ustaz opens by reviewing the last session on the Prophet's ﷺ lineage, then sets the religious and political background before his birth: a Christian but divided Rome, a fire-worshipping Persia, and the Children of Israel and Jews scattered as far as the Hijaz and Yemen. He then tells the story of the Boy and the People of the Ditch (Ashab al-Ukhdud) from the hadith in Sahih Muslim narrated by Suhaib: a boy sent to learn from the royal sorcerer who instead met a monk who taught him tawhid, and who then stood firm before a king who claimed to be God until the people believed. The story is linked to Surah Al-Buruj, and the ustaz begins the transition to the story of Abraha and the People of the Elephant, which connects to Surah Quraysh.
keyPoints: Two stories, the People of the Ditch and the People of the Elephant, help us understand the religious, political and economic climate before the Prophet's ﷺ birth.
Rome was a divided Christian power, while Persia worshipped fire; Mecca lay in the middle between two great powers.
The hadith of Suhaib in Sahih Muslim tells of a boy raised by a monk of tawhid who refused to bow to a king who claimed to be God.
The king used sorcerers to control the people's perception, and sihr means something veiled: reality appears as A while it is really B.
The boy deliberately gave himself up to be killed in the name of Allah so that the whole people would believe, and that is true success.
Surah Al-Buruj warns dictators that every injustice is recorded with Allah.
Scholars differ on the time and place of the People of the Ditch; what matters is its lesson.

chapters.title: Opening and review of the last session
chapters.summary: The ustaz reviews the figures in the Prophet's ﷺ lineage from Prophet Ibrahim to Abdul Muttalib.

chapters.title: Two stories to understand the religious background
chapters.summary: The People of the Ditch and the People of the Elephant are chosen to understand the religious climate before the Prophet's ﷺ birth.

chapters.title: Rome and Persia
chapters.summary: A divided Christian Rome and fire-worshipping Persia as the two great powers.

chapters.title: The Children of Israel, Jews and Christians
chapters.summary: The origin of the names Children of Israel and Jews, and the changes in religion after Prophet Musa AS.

chapters.title: Jews and Christians in the Hijaz and Yemen
chapters.summary: Jews scattered to Yathrib after the dam burst, while Christianity spread to Abyssinia and Yemen.

chapters.title: The king, the sorcerer and the chosen boy
chapters.summary: The hadith of Suhaib begins with a king who claimed to be God and a sorcerer who asked for a boy to train.

chapters.title: The boy meets the monk
chapters.summary: The boy came across a monk who still held to tawhid and began to accept the truth.

chapters.title: Double-meaning speech and solving problems late
chapters.summary: The monk taught the boy half-true answers for the sorcerer and his parents; the ustaz explains the three situations in which tawriyah is allowed.

chapters.title: The beast and the new standing
chapters.summary: The boy tested who was right, killed the beast with a stone, and the monk told him he was now better than he was.

chapters.title: Healing the blind minister
chapters.summary: The boy refused a reward and stressed that only Allah heals; the minister believed and regained his sight.

chapters.title: The king tortures and kills the monk and the minister
chapters.summary: The king tortured the minister, the monk and the minister were sawn in two, but the boy did not budge.

chapters.title: The mountain and the sea
chapters.summary: The soldiers who took the boy up a mountain and out to sea perished, and the boy returned to the palace.

chapters.title: Shooting in the name of Allah
chapters.summary: The boy offered a way to kill him before the whole people, and the people believed in the boy's Lord.

chapters.title: The fiery ditch and Surah Al-Buruj
chapters.summary: The king dug a ditch of fire; the hadith mentions a baby who spoke, and scholars link this story to Surah Al-Buruj.

chapters.title: Abraha and the Negus
chapters.summary: One who escaped the killing reported to Sham, then the Negus sent Aryat and Abraha, and Abraha seized power.

chapters.title: Transition to the People of the Elephant
chapters.summary: The ustaz continues to the story of Abraha and Surah Al-Fil, and mentions scholars' differing views on the time of the Ukhdud story.

people.context: Gathered the Quraysh descendants again to live near the Kaaba.
Had two sons, Ismail and Ishaq; Ishaq's descendants are the Children of Israel.
Also known as Israel; his twelve sons became the twelve tribes of the Children of Israel.
From his name comes the word Jew, and the Quran uses Yahud when condemning deviation.
Narrated the story of the boy and the People of the Ditch from the Prophet ﷺ in Sahih Muslim.
A king of the Jewish religion who considered himself a god, linked to this story.
His name is not mentioned in the hadith; some sirah books say Abdullah. He appears as a believing boy who sacrificed himself so the people would know Allah.
A follower of Prophet Isa AS who still held to tawhid, taught the boy in secret and was sawn in two for defending his faith.
Complained to the Prophet ﷺ about the torture in Mecca, and was reminded of the story of earlier peoples.
Was forced to say words he did not believe when tortured, then a verse came down permitting it.
Received instructions from Constantinople and sent an army against the king of Yemen.
Sent by the Negus against the tyrannical king in Yemen and took over the government.
General Aryat, who later staged a coup; his story continues with the People of the Elephant.
Cited for the view that the People of the Ditch story took place about 46 years before the Prophet ﷺ was born.
Cited for the view that burning people alive took place in many places.

lessons.title: Religion as decoration for corrupt rulers
lessons.body: Corrupt kings brand their governments with religion to win the people's support, while in reality they are rotten.

lessons.title: Sorcery as perception control
lessons.body: Sihr means something veiled, where reality looks like A but is really B; power controls information so that people believe what is not the truth.

lessons.title: The fitrah recognises the truth
lessons.body: Although raised in an environment where the king was considered a god, the boy felt the truth of tawhid through his fitrah.

lessons.title: Guard worship from interference
lessons.body: The ustaz stresses that matters of worship must be guarded; opening the door to practices the Prophet ﷺ and the Companions did not do leads to deviation.

lessons.title: Simple tawhid without intermediaries
lessons.body: The monk taught simple tawhid: worship Allah, humans are not gods, and there is no intermediary.

lessons.title: When faith touches the heart
lessons.body: The boy was willing to be late and beaten to seek knowledge of tawhid even though a post at the palace was guaranteed.

lessons.title: Double-meaning speech in three situations
lessons.body: Giving an answer that is not wholly true is allowed in war, between husband and wife, and in reconciling people who quarrel.

lessons.title: Think of the public interest
lessons.body: The boy acted to remove the beast because he thought of the public who could not pass.

lessons.title: Strategy for keeping da'wah secret
lessons.body: The monk told the boy not to reveal where he was if caught, to protect the religion taught in secret.

lessons.title: Don't sell faith for wealth
lessons.body: The boy refused the minister's expensive gifts because his aim was to bring people to Islam, and his conscience was clear.

lessons.title: Steadfastness under torture
lessons.body: This story inspired the Companions who would go through torture in Mecca; our safe situation should be appreciated.

lessons.title: Change begins with the sacrifice of a few
lessons.body: Usually change begins when one or two people start by sacrificing, and ignite change.

lessons.title: A goal beyond this world
lessons.body: The boy was willing to be killed because he wanted everyone who witnessed it to believe.

lessons.title: Every injustice is recorded with Allah
lessons.body: Burj means watchtower; Allah records every deed even when nobody witnesses or defends.

lessons.title: Success from Allah's perspective
lessons.body: Those who died in this story were thought to have failed, but Allah changes the perspective by calling them the ones who won.

glossary.meaning: In Arabic means something veiled, where reality A appears but is really B.
A boy of about 13 to 19, equivalent to a lower-secondary student.
Those who dug a ditch and burned the believers, mentioned in Surah Al-Buruj.
A follower of Prophet Isa AS who still held to tawhid and worshipped in seclusion.
The original state of humans, who recognise the truth.
A statement with two meanings: true according to the speaker's intention but understood differently by the listener.
A large four-legged dangerous animal that blocked traffic in the hadith.
A large saw used to split the heads of the monk and the minister.
Towers or watchtowers; the name of Surah Al-Buruj, depicting Allah who records everything.

dalil.context: The ustaz says Allah states in the Quran that Christians are closer to Muslims than Jews. The verse number is not mentioned. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: You [Prophet] are sure to find that the most hostile to the believers are the Jews and those who associate other deities with God; you are sure to find that the closest in affection towards the believers are those who say, ‘We are Christians,’ for there are among them people devoted to learning and ascetics. These people are not given to arrogance,

dalil.context: The ustaz says this story is sahih and narrated by Suhaib ar-Rumi in Sahih Muslim. It is linked to Surah Al-Buruj according to many exegetes.
dalil.translation: The Prophet ﷺ narrated that before you there was a king who had a sorcerer. When the sorcerer grew old, he asked for a boy to teach. The boy met a monk who taught him tawhid, and was granted the ability to heal the sick by Allah's leave. The king tortured the monk and the believing minister, but the boy stayed firm. Finally the boy showed how to kill him by shooting an arrow and saying the name of this boy's Lord; the people believed and the king dug a ditch of fire to burn them.

dalil.context: The ustaz explains this when explaining the monk's advice to the boy, counted as tawriyah, an answer with a double meaning.
dalil.translation: In the Shariah, three situations are allowed in which the truth need not be stated fully: in war, between husband and wife, and when reconciling people who quarrel.

dalil.context: The ustaz mentions this hadith to show that the boy's story is authentic and strengthened the Companions when tested in Mecca.
dalil.translation: When Khabbab ibn al-Aratt complained to the Prophet ﷺ about torture, he reminded him that people before them had their heads sawn in two, and others were combed with iron combs until their flesh was torn from the bone.

dalil.context: The ustaz refers to the verse revealed when Ammar ibn Yasir was forced to say words of disbelief with his tongue though his heart did not mean them. The verse number is not mentioned. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: With the exception of those who are forced to say they do not believe, although their hearts remain firm in faith, those who reject God after believing in Him and open their hearts to disbelief will have the wrath of God upon them and a grievous punishment awaiting them.

dalil.context: The ustaz reads the beginning of Surah Al-Buruj while linking it to the story of the People of the Ditch.

sirah.era: Before the Prophet's ﷺ birth: the religious and political climate around Mecca
sirah.summary: This lecture sets the background of great powers, religion and geopolitics around Mecca before the Prophet's ﷺ birth, through the story of the People of the Ditch and the beginning of Abraha's story.
